newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia accused of media crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Serbia accused of media crackdown.

text.p: An independent Serbian newspaper on Friday accused Serbian authorities of cracking down on media freedom and harassment of the independent press ahead of crucial Serbian elections later this year.

The Belgrade newspaper Nasa Borba said in a commentary to be published on Saturday it had been ordered by Serbia's Public Revenue Department to pay new taxes even though it had already met its tax bill this year.

Calling the tax order a "state racket", the paper said: "if today we agree to pay the fabricated unpaid taxes, tomorrow they will levy taxes because we are not all dark haired or do not all wear the same size shoes."

The Public Revenue Department ordered Nasa Borba to pay 437,000 dinars (132,000 German marks) in tax although it said it had already paid 341,000 dinars in turnover tax and another 379,000 dinars in income tax on fees and and wages since the beginning of the year.
The order followed a lightning inspection of Fininvest of Novi Sad, the publishers of Nasa Borba, last week by a five-member public revenue department team.

Fininvest director Dusan Malesevic has written to Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic to point out that the firm has fully met its tax obligations to date, adding that the inspectors completely ignored the documents presented to them.
He described the "incomprehensible and illegal gesture of the inspectors as serious pressure by the authorities on Nasa Borba and independent media as a whole which threatens press freedom."
Malesevic said this coincided with the award to the daily of the prestigious Golden Pen award by the International Publishers Association.
"Since its establishment in February 1995 Nasa Borba has been a thorn in the eye of the authorities," the paper said in its commentary which was made available to Reuters.
Opposition parties have accused the authorities of clamping down on media freedom ahead of an election for the Serbian presidency and parliament due by the end of the year.
Belgrade has come under severe pressure by the United States to improve its human rights and press freedom record.
Washington has said improvement of these would help dismantle an outer wall of sanctions against Belgrade barring it from international financial and political organisations.
State authorities deny stifling media freedom claiming there were some 2,500 media organisations in the country.
Independent Belgrade student Radio Index went off the air on Friday morning owing to heavy interference, news programme editor Aleksandar Vasic told BK TV.
He said the interference was intentional and the station would be using another transmitter over the next few days.

Radio Index and B92 Radio played a vital role in three months of demonstrations this winter when thousands took to the streets protesting against local elections fraud which they said robbed the opposition of victory in Serbia's 14 biggest cities.
Radio B92 was taken off the air briefly during the protests but was allowed to broadcast again after international pressure.
Independent BK Television has been experiencing similar problems over the past few months.
